unit.title: Inside the stock exchange
unit.description: What a stock exchange is, who trades on it, how prices are set and how the Spanish one works

texts: Who are you buying from?
Laura
I want to buy Inditex shares. I buy them from Inditex, right?
Who does Laura buy her shares from?
From Inditex, since it's the owner
Not day to day. Inditex only gets money when it issues new shares.
From another investor who wants to sell
That's it! The exchange brings buyers and sellers together.
From the exchange, which keeps shares in stock
The exchange doesn't hold shares: it just matches buy and sell orders.
So how do I get to the exchange?
Through an authorised **broker**: they take your order to the market.
Every time you buy, someone sells. What might they know that you don't?
What's a stock exchange for?
A **stock exchange** is a regulated market where shares, bonds and ETFs are bought and sold. What does it do, and what doesn't it?
The exchange does it
It doesn't do that
Help a company raise money to grow
By selling shares or bonds to investors, without taking out a loan.
Let you sell your shares whenever you want
That's **liquidity**: the exchange brings buyers and sellers together every day.
Guarantee that shares go up
The exchange promises nothing about the price: it just makes buying and selling possible.
Give every security a public price
Everyone sees the same price, at every moment.
Guarantee shares a minimum price
The price can fall as far as people's appetite to buy falls.
Apply the same rules to everyone
It's an organised market: equal rules and public prices for all.
Sort the six cards.
An exchange **brings buyers and sellers together**, with equal rules and public prices. It serves companies and investors, but guarantees nothing about the price.
Hint: the exchange organises the market, but doesn't promise profits.
You're doing really well! Nearly there.
Tap each card: does the exchange do it or not?

steps.title: Who's who
steps.body:
In Spain the stock exchange is run by **BME** (Bolsas y Mercados Españoles), part of the Swiss SIX group, and supervised by the **CNMV** (Spain's securities regulator).

You don't go to the exchange yourself: you buy through an authorised **broker**, who takes your order to the market.
steps.key: The exchange is the meeting point; the broker is the way in.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, look up Inditex: everyone sees that same price.

texts: Who's on the other side?
When you buy a share, someone sells it to you. Who could it be? Sort each one.
Individual (retail)
Professional
A student investing €50 a month from their app
A **retail investor**: an individual investing their own money.
A pension plan
An **institutional investor**: it moves the money of thousands of people.
An algorithm that trades in microseconds
That's **high-frequency trading**: buying and selling at speeds no person could match.
Someone who always quotes a buying price and a selling price
A **market maker**: they earn the difference between the two prices.
A central bank buying bonds
Central banks and governments trade in bonds and currencies.
Your aunt, who buys a bit of a fund every month
Another retail investor: she invests her own money, in small amounts.
Sort the six participants.
On the other side of your order there are usually **professionals** with more information, better tools and almost zero costs. That's why beating them in the short term is so hard.
Hint: if it moves lots of people's money or it's a machine, it's professional.
Look how many kinds of professionals there are in the market.
Tap each card: individual or professional?
Beating them on speed
Bruno
A share has dropped 8 % in minutes after its results.
I'm going to buy and sell all afternoon and beat the algorithms!
What do you tell Bruno?
Go for it: if he's quick, he'll win
The algorithms reacted in microseconds. Bruno will always be too late.
His edge isn't speed, it's time
That's it! He can wait for years and keep his costs really low.
Let him, but with a small amount
He loses less, but he's still in a race he can't win.
So we small investors don't count for anything?
In the long run you're not competing with them: you share in what companies earn.

steps.title: Your edge
steps.body: A retail investor doesn't have to report every quarter, can wait for years and can keep costs very low. That's their edge, not speed.
steps.key: The stock market is full of professionals: your edge is time and low costs.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, add a company you'd hold for years to your Favourites.

texts: Thursday, 20:00 in Spain
Each market has its own hours. It's Thursday and it's **20:00** (Spanish mainland time). What's open?
Open
Closed
Madrid Stock Exchange
Open from 9:00 to 17:30: it closed hours ago.
New York Stock Exchange
9:30 to 16:00 local time: **15:30 to 22:00** in Spain.
London Stock Exchange
8:00 to 16:30 local time: 9:00 to 17:30 in Spain.
Bitcoin
Crypto trades 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, bank holidays included.
The euro against the dollar
Currencies trade 24 hours a day, from Sunday night to Friday night.
Tokyo Stock Exchange
It opens in the middle of the night in Spain.
Frankfurt Stock Exchange
Like Madrid and Paris: 9:00 to 17:30.
Sort the seven markets.
**Madrid, 9:00 to 17:30; New York, 15:30 to 22:00** Spanish time. Crypto never closes and currencies only close at the weekend.
Hint: New York opens in the afternoon in Spain and closes at 22:00.
At this time, almost all of Europe has already closed.
Tap each market: open or closed?
An order at 23:00
Pablo
It's 23:00 in Spain. New York closed an hour ago.
A US company has just posted amazing results! I'm buying right now at market.
What will happen to Pablo's order?
It executes right away, at the closing price
With the exchange closed there's nobody to match it with: it waits for the open.
It waits for the open and could cost a lot more
Exactly. If it opens with a **gap** up, he pays much more than he sees.
It cancels itself because it's night-time
It usually stays pending until the open, at whatever the price is then.
A gap?
A jump in price between the close and the open, with no prices in between.

steps.title: Watch the clock
steps.body:
Because of the **clock change**, the US and Europe don't change their clocks on the same day: for a few weeks a year New York opens at **14:30** Spanish time.

Tokyo opens in the middle of the night in Spain and takes a lunch break (Tokyo time).
steps.key: Before you trade, check whether the market is open.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, check whether Apple shows «open» or «closed» right now.

texts: Zero fees and a bonus
Marta
Check out this broker: 0 fees and a welcome bonus.
It's not on the CNMV registers and has no European passport. Does that matter?
What do you tell Marta?
Open an account: zero fees can't be beaten
If it's an unauthorised firm, she could lose everything, with no regulator to turn to.
Look for an authorised broker
Exactly. Authorised by the CNMV or by another EU regulator.
Try it with just €500
She could lose that €500 too. And they usually ask for more later.
So what exactly does a broker do?
It receives your order, takes it to the market and charges you fees.
What if something goes wrong?
Once you buy, your shares are **registered in your name**, kept separate from the broker's own assets. What protects you and what doesn't?
You're protected
That's your risk
Your broker goes bust, but your shares are in your name
The **custodian** keeps them separate from the broker's assets: they're still yours.
A Spanish broker goes bust and some of what's yours is missing
The **FOGAIN** (Spain's investor guarantee fund) steps in, up to €100,000 per investor.
Your shares fall 30 % on the market
FOGAIN doesn't cover market falls: they're your risk.
An unregistered scam firm vanishes with your money
Without authorisation there's no regulator and no guarantee fund.
The company you invested in goes bust
That's the risk of your investment, not of the broker: nobody gives it back.
Sort the five cases.
Your securities are held **in your name**. **FOGAIN** covers up to €100,000 if the firm can't give you back what's yours, **not if the market falls**.
Hint: the guarantee fund protects you from the firm, not from the market.
Notice: what the market does to your money is your own risk.
Does it protect you or is it your risk? Tap each case

steps.title: Settlement and custody
steps.body:
Once matched, the trade **settles**: the money goes to the seller and the shares to you. In Europe it takes two business days (**T+2**) and will move to one (T+1) on 11 October 2027; in the US it has been one since 2024. In Spain the central register is **Iberclear**.

With a broker from another EU country, that country's fund covers you, and it may cover less (the EU minimum is €20,000). Before you open an account, check on the CNMV website that the broker is authorised.
steps.key: The broker is your way in; your securities are held in your name.
steps.tip: Try it: make a purchase in Market and find the trade in your Portfolio.

texts: The trendy listing
Bruno
Everyone's talking about a fashion brand going public.
If it's going public it must be doing brilliantly, right? I'm putting in all my savings!
What do you advise him?
Put it all in: it's a one-off opportunity
If it falls 30 % in the first few months, he's left with no cushion and with losses.
Read the prospectus and, if he invests, only a small part
Exactly. The **prospectus**, approved by the CNMV, explains the business and the risks.
Wait and see what people say on social media
Social media doesn't know the company. The prospectus does.
The price is set by whoever's selling, and they know the company better than you.
Many listings end up trading below their offer price.
Who gets your money?
In the **primary market** new securities are issued. In the **secondary market**, investors buy and sell existing ones among themselves.
The issuer (primary)
Another investor (secondary)
A company raises capital with new shares
It issues new shares: the money goes to the company.
You buy 10 Iberdrola shares from your app
You buy them from another investor: Iberdrola gets nothing.
A stock market listing with newly issued shares
New shares: the money goes into the company.
You sell your shares to another investor
Something that already exists changes hands.
The Treasury auctions bills
New securities: the money goes to the state, which is the issuer.
You buy a government bond that's already trading
It already existed: you buy it from another investor.
Sort the six transactions.
**Primary:** new securities are issued and the money goes to the issuer. **Secondary:** existing ones change hands and the company gets nothing.
Ask yourself: does whoever issues the security get new money?
The everyday stock market is almost all secondary market.
Tap each transaction: primary or secondary?
OPS or OPV?
There are two ways to go public in Spain, often combined. The key: **who keeps the money?**
OPS: it goes to the company
OPV: it goes to the selling owners
New shares are created to open factories
Public **subscription** offer (OPS): new shares, money for the company.
The founder sells some of her shares
Public **sale** offer (OPV): she sells something that already exists and the money is hers.
A fund that bought in years ago sells its stake
The current owners sell: the company gets nothing.
The company issues shares to pay off its debt
It issues new shares: the money goes to the company.
Sort the four cases.

**OPS:** new shares and money for the company. **OPV:** the owners sell and the money goes to them. Outside Spain, a listing is simply called an IPO. Try it: in Market, open a company's monthly chart and find its first day on the stock market.
If no new shares are created, the company doesn't get paid.
Before a listing, check who's selling and why.
Tap each case: OPS or OPV?

u5l7.title: The Spanish stock market: the IBEX and the continuous market

texts: Out of the IBEX
Pablo
The company I own shares in has dropped out of the IBEX 35. Is it doing terribly?
What do you tell Pablo?
Yes: only the best companies are in the IBEX
It has the 35 **most liquid** ones, not the best.
Not necessarily: it's just traded less than others now
Exactly. Not being in the IBEX doesn't make it a bad company.
It's no longer listed
It's still trading on the continuous market, with over a hundred companies.
And who decides that?
A technical committee, twice a year: in June and December.
Where is it listed?
Over a hundred companies trade on the **continuous market**, but not all in the same shop window.
IBEX 35
BME Growth
Latibex
A big power company with millions of shares traded every day
It's among the 35 most liquid: it's in the IBEX.
A small tech start-up looking to grow
**BME Growth**: small, expanding companies, with fewer requirements and more risk.
A Mexican company that wants to trade in euros
**Latibex** brings together Latin American companies trading in euros.
A big, heavily traded Spanish bank
Lots of liquidity: it's one of the 35 that make up the IBEX.
A small, expanding family business
Small and expanding: it fits BME Growth (formerly MAB).
Place the five companies.
The **IBEX 35** is the shop window; the continuous market is the whole shop. **BME Growth** has small companies and more risk, and **Latibex** Latin American ones.
Hint: the IBEX goes by liquidity; BME Growth, by small size.
Size, liquidity and origin decide the segment.
Tap each company: where is it listed?

steps.title: The IBEX 35 and the continuous market
steps.body:
The **continuous market** (SIBE) links the Madrid, Barcelona, Bilbao and Valencia exchanges in one electronic system, with a single order book per security. It's run by **BME**, part of the Swiss SIX group since 2020.

The **IBEX 35** is weighted by market capitalisation, counting only freely traded shares. Its base was **3,000 points** at the end of 1989.
steps.key: The IBEX 35 is the shop window; the continuous market is the whole shop.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, use «Explore by index» and look at the 35 IBEX companies.

options: A regulated market where buy and sell orders for securities are matched
A bank that looks after your savings
A company that sells you its own shares every day
u5l1-1.explanation: The exchange matches orders: it brings buyers and sellers together with public rules and prices.

u5l1-4.prompt: Match each name with its role.
u5l1-4.explanation: Market, regulator, intermediary and company: four different roles.
right: Supervises the securities markets in Spain

options: Uses a broker authorised by the CNMV
Goes to the Madrid Stock Exchange building to buy them
u5l1-7.explanation: You access the stock market through an authorised intermediary, never through messages from strangers.
feedback: The shares are held in her name, with a supervised intermediary.
The exchange doesn't deal with individuals: you always trade through an intermediary.
Most likely that money never comes back: nobody buys shares via Bizum.

u5l1-9.prompt: Quick: who supervises the securities markets in Spain?
u5l1-9.explanation: The Comisión Nacional del Mercado de Valores, Spain's securities regulator.

u5l1-10.prompt: A stock exchange applies the same rules and public prices to all participants.
u5l1-10.explanation: That's why it's an organised, transparent market.

u5l2-1.explanation: Each participant has different goals and tools.

u5l2-2.prompt: How does a market maker make money?
options: From the dividends of the companies it trades
By charging the CNMV a fee
From the difference between its buying and selling prices
u5l2-2.explanation: It buys a little cheaper than it sells: that difference is its margin.

u5l2-3.explanation: Institutional investors invest the money of thousands of people.

u5l2-7.prompt: A retail investor competes on equal terms with professionals in information and speed.
u5l2-7.explanation: Professionals have more data, better tools and almost zero costs.

u5l2-8.prompt: What advantages does a retail investor have in the long term? Select all that apply.
options: Doesn't need to make money every quarter
Can wait for years without answering to anyone
u5l2-8.explanation: Information and speed aren't on their side. Patience is: they don't answer to anyone each quarter and can wait for years. And they can keep costs very low too.

u5l2-9.prompt: Every time you buy a share, another investor ____ it.
u5l2-9.explanation: Every purchase has a sale on the other side.

u5l4-1.prompt: Match each market with its hours (Spanish mainland time).
u5l4-1.explanation: Each market has its own hours; crypto never closes.

u5l4-4.prompt: What time does the New York Stock Exchange normally open in Spanish mainland time?
u5l4-4.explanation: From 9:30 to 16:00 in New York = from 15:30 to 22:00 in Spain.

u5l4-6.prompt: Because of the clock change, for a few weeks a year New York opens at 14:30 Spanish time.
u5l4-6.explanation: The US and Europe don't put their clocks forward or back on the same day.

u5l4-8.prompt: On a Tuesday at 10:00 (Spanish mainland time), open or closed?
u5l4-8.explanation: At 10:00 in Spain, New York hasn't opened yet and Tokyo has already closed.

u5l4-10.prompt: When a share opens far from the previous close because of overnight news, it's called a ____.
u5l4-10.explanation: A gap is a jump in price with no trades in between.

options: Guarantees that your investments go up
Takes your order to the market
u5l5-1.explanation: It's the intermediary between you and the market.

u5l5-4.prompt: Quick: up to how much does FOGAIN cover per investor?
u5l5-4.explanation: Up to €100,000 per investor, if the Spanish firm can't give you back what's yours.

u5l5-5.prompt: Put the journey of your buy order in order.
options: The shares are registered in your name
It settles in two business days
You place the order in the app
The broker takes it to the market
u5l5-5.explanation: From the app to the register: that's how the shares become yours.

u5l5-7.prompt: Match each name with its function.
u5l5-7.explanation: Each piece protects one part of the process.
right: Holds your securities in your name
Takes your order to the market

u5l5-8.prompt: In Europe, a share purchase settles in ____ business days.
u5l5-8.explanation: T+2: the trade date plus two business days. From 11 October 2027 it will be one (T+1).

u5l5-10.prompt: Pablo has €60,000 with a broker based in another EU country and assumes he's covered by Spain's FOGAIN. What does he do?
options: Nothing: all guarantee funds are the same
Checks which guarantee fund applies to him and how much it covers
Takes it all out and keeps it at home
u5l5-10.explanation: The protection depends on the firm's country: check before opening an account.
feedback: They aren't: the EU minimum is €20,000 and each country sets its own.
He finds out he's covered by the broker's home-country fund, with a different limit: now he knows where he stands.
At home there's no protection at all, and he also loses purchasing power.

u5l6-1.prompt: Match each term with what it means.
u5l6-1.explanation: Knowing who receives the money is the key to telling them apart.
right: The owners sell; the money goes to them
Investors buying and selling among themselves
Information and risks approved by the CNMV
New shares; the money goes to the company

u5l6-3.prompt: Today you buy Inditex shares on the stock market. Who gets your money?
options: The investor selling them to you
Inditex, the company that owns the shares
u5l6-3.explanation: It's the secondary market: Inditex gets nothing from that purchase.

u5l6-4.prompt: In a pure OPV, the company receives no new money: the selling shareholders do.
u5l6-4.explanation: If the company wants new money, it has to issue shares (OPS).

u5l6-6.prompt: Which document should you read before taking part in a listing?
options: The comments about it on social media
The prospectus approved by the CNMV
u5l6-6.explanation: The prospectus explains the business, the accounts and the risks.

u5l6-8.prompt: When an already listed company issues new shares to raise money, it carries out a capital ____.
u5l6-8.explanation: A capital increase is the primary market even though the company is already listed.

u5l6-9.prompt: Put the steps of a stock market listing in order.
options: Investors apply for shares at the set price
First day of trading on the secondary market
The company decides to go public
u5l6-9.explanation: After the debut, the shares are traded between investors.

u5l7-1.prompt: Match each name with what it is.
u5l7-1.explanation: The Spanish stock market has several segments with different rules and risks.
right: Electronic system linking the four exchanges

u5l7-2.prompt: How often is the IBEX 35 line-up reviewed in the ordinary course?
options: Never: it's always the same companies
u5l7-2.explanation: In June and December a technical committee decides what comes in and what goes out.

u5l7-7.prompt: The IBEX 35 started from a base of ____ points at the end of 1989.
u5l7-7.explanation: That base is the yardstick for how much it has risen or fallen.

u5l7-8.prompt: Pablo wants to put almost all his savings into a BME Growth company because «it could multiply». What does he bear in mind?
options: That they tend to be smaller, less liquid and riskier
That BME Growth guarantees the investment
That it's just as liquid as an IBEX company
u5l7-8.explanation: Small company: more potential, but also more risk and less liquidity.
feedback: If he invests, he does it with a small part, knowing it may be hard to sell.
No segment of the stock market guarantees anything.
No: with low volume, selling quickly may force him to cut the price a lot.

u5l7-9.prompt: How does the IBEX 35 weight its companies?
options: They all weigh exactly the same
u5l7-9.explanation: The biggest companies by market value carry more weight in the index.

u5l2-11.prompt: Leo invests €50 a month in an index fund. A friend tells him he'll never beat the professionals that way and should trade every day. What does he do?
options: Sticks to his plan: he has time and low costs
Stops investing: the stock market is only for professionals
Starts trading every day to beat them
u5l2-11.explanation: The temptation is to trade more, but in the short term the retail investor is at a disadvantage. In the long term, time and low costs work in his favour.
feedback: He doesn't compete on speed: for years he shares in what companies earn.
He gives up his big advantage, time. In the long run he doesn't need to beat them on speed.
He joins a race where algorithms and professionals have the edge, and pays costs on every trade.

u5l4-11.prompt: Leo works from 9:00 to 18:00 and wants to buy Microsoft shares while the New York Stock Exchange is open. When can he do it on a normal day?
u5l4-11.explanation: New York opens in the afternoon Spanish time, from 15:30 to 22:00. Buying outside those hours is tempting because it's convenient, but the order waits for the open and may fill at a different price.
feedback: At midnight New York has already closed: the order would execute the next day, at whatever the price is then.
At 14:00 New York hasn't opened yet: the order would wait for the open.
New York is open from 15:30 to 22:00 Spanish time: he has plenty of time in the evening.

u5l6-11.prompt: A company announces its stock market listing. The prospectus says all the shares on offer belong to its founders, who are selling part of their stake. What does that mean?
options: It's an OPS: the company gets money to grow
It's an OPV: the money goes to the founders
It's a good sign: if they're listing, it must be doing great
u5l6-11.explanation: If no new shares are issued, it's an OPV and the company gets nothing. The temptation is to read it as a good sign, but whoever sells picks the moment that suits them.
feedback: In an OPS new shares are issued. Here only existing shares change hands.
No new shares are created: the company receives nothing. It's worth asking why they're selling now.
Whoever sells knows the company better than you and picks the moment that suits them.
